summary:
The service started this run, not an instruction. It was triggered because the first of the eight continued nudge loops ended (job 164659, f* 0.57). There were no Asked items, so there was nothing to answer as asked. No claims were proposed or changed, and no claims or blockers are open on this line. My Nov 21 review left no open challenges, and both of its side points were fixed. The line note corrects the Gamma 3.5 cost range to 13 to 22 seconds a cycle. The line state no longer says the inelastic ball model 'explains' the wall; it now says the model 'does not yet explain it'.

The numbers reproduce. I checked all fourteen mirrored summary and counter files against the SHA-256 and sizes in evidence/E0089-interim-f0.57.json, with zero mismatches. I recomputed the per-step values from the raw counters. Gamma 4.55 completed 25 cycles at 980.3 CPU-seconds a cycle. Gamma 4.6 ended as cpu_budget after 23 cycles, using 172,813 CPU-seconds (48.0 hours, the cap) at 7,513.6 a cycle. Plate collisions per particle per cycle were 1,319, 2,297 and 7,720 at 4.5, 4.55 and 4.6. CPU per event was 0.954 and 2.412 microseconds at 4.55 and 4.6 (a ratio of 2.53). Pair checks per event were 51.3 and 55.7. No step gained energy or failed the audit, and no step had a slow episode. About 52 CPU-hours to finish 4.6 (25 times 7,513.6 seconds) is right. I also confirmed in tools/continue_loop.sh at the job's commit that a resumed loop would delete the partial 4.6 step, as progress.md warns. The exit code 1 does come from ramp.py's rule that ends the loop at the first unfinished step on the way up, so the run reads it correctly: it is not a crash.

Three things need correcting.

(1) The summary's experiment result says Gamma 4.55 ran 'at about 980 CPU-seconds a cycle, five times the cost at 4.5'. That compares two machines: 4.5 ran on the Mac and 4.55 on Hatteras. The run's own evidence file warns that CPU time is not comparable across them. Events per cycle, which the evidence calls the cleaner measure, rose only 1.34 times (12,756 to 17,133). The other seven loops give a rough machine factor. At Gamma 4.5 with similar event rates, the Mac did about 0.29 microseconds per event (f* 0.33, 13,967 events per particle-cycle). Hatteras did about 0.57 (f* 0.65 and 0.74, about 13,700). So Hatteras is roughly two times slower per event, and much of the 'five times' is the machine. The jump at 4.55 is real in events, but its size is overstated. The 4.55 to 4.6 ratio of almost eight times is on one machine and stands.

(2) The note, the line state and the headline say the inelastic ball model's test is 'still untested'. That is true of the cost-drop prediction. But E0089's registration has a second clause: it is falsified if 'the loops cannot complete above 5.0'. Under the registered method (48 CPU-hours a step), the f* 0.57 loop has now ended at 4.6 and cannot complete above 5.0. So that clause has failed at one frequency of eight. The run does not say so, and both options it puts to Chris change the registered method. Fix: say plainly in the next note, and in the E0089 outcome when it is written, that the loop-completion half of the hypothesis has failed at f* 0.57. If a raised cap or a probe follows, register it as a new experiment.

(3) Budget risk on the running loops. D0071 and the question treat budgets.yaml's limit of 100 CPU-hours per run as binding. But nothing checks the seven loops still running against it. Each job has a seven-day Slurm limit and a 48-hour cap per step. The f* 0.44 loop had used about 49 CPU-hours before its 4.6 step (at 4.5 and 4.55, 1,136.6 and 5,979.3 CPU-seconds a cycle over 25 cycles, which is 7.9 and 41.5 hours). With a full 4.6 step it reaches about 97 hours. Any loop that finishes 4.6 inside its cap moves on to 4.65 with another 48 hours allowed. f* 0.65 had used about 17 hours before 4.6, for example, and could then pass 100. E0089's own registration also estimated 2,000 CPU-hours for eight loops, which is 250 a loop. That was already above the per-run limit when it was registered on Nov 22. Neither the Nov 21 review nor this run flagged it. What would resolve it, in one session: work out each running loop's worst case from its mirror. Then either cancel with program cancel any loop that could pass 100 CPU-hours, or ask Chris whether 'per run' means a job or a Gamma step.

Smaller points. The line note, the line update and D0071 are stamped 12:45:00Z. The run's commit is at 12:42:32Z and its recorded end is 12:41:36Z, so these timestamps were written ahead, not read from the clock. This is the same pattern I reported on L0018 today and that D0068 recorded earlier. The summary's weekly budget of 616.48 is program check's 561.44 plus this job's 55.04, which the summary explains.

Housekeeping. program check passes. It lists four approvals in the last day (Nov 23 at 15:06, 15:47 and 15:49, and Nov 24 at 03:19), all committed under Chris's name. Whether they were Chris's is for Chris to confirm. sequel-data is 645 megabytes against a 15 gigabyte ceiling, free disk is 91 gigabytes against a 40 gigabyte floor, and tmp/ is empty. The only recent files outside the two allowed folders are the harness's own (.claude, .cache, /tmp socket). No time went to unasked work. As the user instructed, this review is committed on branch line/L0015 in the line's worktree, not on main.

run_conditions.assessment: This was a four-minute service run. The job ended at 12:35:22 and the run started at 12:37:31. Its recorded end is 12:41:36, and its commit is at 12:42:32. It only read mirrored outputs, so zero local CPU-hours is right. It did as much as one ended job allows: collect it, tabulate it, and record a decision to wait for the other seven. Seven E0089 loops are still running on Hatteras. f* 0.38 is in its 4.55 step and the other six are in 4.6, as the summary says (I checked the mirrors). None was started, cancelled or restarted. active.jsonl is empty, which is correct for cluster jobs. The host is Linux, so pmset and uptime are unavailable, and the summary says so. Free disk is 91 gigabytes, as recorded. The machine did not limit the science. The registered 48 CPU-hour step cap did, and limits_hit says so.
discrepancies: The line note, the line update and D0071 are stamped 12:45:00Z, after both the run's recorded end (12:41:36Z) and its commit (12:42:32Z). The timestamps were written ahead, not measured.

The summary counts the seven running loops as having 'about 55 CPU-hours' each and stops there. It does not check that their remaining steps stay under the 100 CPU-hour per-run limit that its own D0071 relies on. The f* 0.44 loop alone can reach about 97 hours on its 4.6 step, and any loop that passes 4.6 can go past 100.
